pass_a.49: Besides the wandering off from the argument, Placeus says there are still other faults in the three replies of Doctor Garissoles, and he will mark them in a few words. First: Garissoles claims we insist there was a definite reason why the Apostle spoke of that imputation. For once Paul had said that by one man's sin death was brought into the world, it could be asked where that sin got such force that it dragged so great an evil not onto one or another person but onto all. Paul's answer, on Garissoles's telling, is that this came about because by that one sin all were made liable, or because when that one sinned all are to be understood to have sinned in him and with him. Placeus's charge: this reply does not touch the nerve of the argument; it makes the Apostle trifling; with nothing but changed wording it answers the very thing that was being asked; and as the cause of the effect it brings forward the effect itself whose cause was sought. For what does 'sin entered into the world' mean to the author of this reply? Nothing except that actual sin was imputed to all men. That is clearest from Garissoles's own chapter 8, section 8, page 217, and from some other places. What again does 'all sinned in Adam' mean to him? He says it cannot be better expounded than by saying Adam's sin is imputed to all — same chapter, section 10, page 222. So to someone asking why Adam's actual sin is imputed to all unto death, the Apostle would have answered: because it is imputed to all. To someone asking where that sin gets the force to be imputed not to one or another but to all, he answers that it came about because it is imputed to all. What is trifling, if this is not?
pass_a.50: To those two faults a third is also added: Garissoles contradicts himself. If the Apostle's mind was what this reply attributes to him, then the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον must be construed after all the antecedents — sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death pervaded into all — because they would then answer a question that could arise from those immediately preceding words. That overturns the rendering 'in which.' For once that rendering is assumed, the words 'in which all sinned' must be construed before all those antecedents: they cohere at once with the noun ἀνθρώπου, and there is a transposition. So the construction would have to be: As through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death pervaded into all men. Locked Greek lemma: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ / ἥμαρτον — do not revive the OCR misread ἔργον.
pass_a.51: Second Garissoles reply: same fault of missing the argument; he also mishandles the so-called uncertain cause, and some of his wording is off. He asks how anyone can call Paul's cause uncertain when 1 Corinthians 15:22 climbs all the way to Adam the protoplast and declares that we all die in Adam. Placeus presses the relevance: does that verse supply a reason why all die by virtue of their communion with Adam? And must 'in Adam all die' be read even in the imputative sense of the opposing school? What comes next is worse. Garissoles claims that in neither passage does Paul attend to particular causes lodged in each human individual as the grounds of dying; he rather lays down a genus-wide cause that bears equally on all, etc. That talk treats hereditary corruption as if it were not already such a genus-wide cause — though it is no less shared than the death of sinners, than human nature itself, or than the imputation they promote. Step by step, then, the reformers' hard-won teaching on the force and guilt of hereditary corruption is set aside and almost erased, to clear space for an imputation those same great men either never taught or actively refuted.
pass_a.52: Garissoles next denies it is fair to label the cause remote and distant: what matters here, he says, is not centuries of time but how efficacious the thing is. Placeus counters with a question: can an injustice that never lodged in me, but only in Adam who died millennia before I was, stand as equally immediate and proximate to me or my death as the injustice that clings in my inmost self and that all confess as my death's cause? Adam's sin was followed by corruption, and corruption by death; so corruption sits nearer to death than the sin confined to Adam alone. Garissoles also claims that people who derive corruption from Adam do not therefore treat Adam as remote, because blood-union with him is nearest even if personal union is not. Placeus reverses that: they do treat him as remote and distant — meaning first — as the fountain from which corruption streamed to everyone else. Distinguishing blood from person so as to call our nearest Adam-union a blood matter rather than a personal one leaves Placeus unpersuaded. Blood differs from blood and nature from nature by the same numerical (not specific) difference that divides person from person. I received my person through the chain of intermediate parents from Adam, and my nature the same way. Adam is first father, not nearest father; nothing reached me from him except through my nearest parents.
pass_a.53: Garissoles's comparison-move: because Paul pairs Christ with Adam, Adam's disobedience should no more be called remote to condemnation than Christ's obedience is remote to justification. Placeus rejects the hidden premise that two first-in-kind causes of opposite effects may be compared only if both are equally proximate. Christ's obedience is known to be the full and sole ground of justification; Adam's disobedience is only a partial, incomplete ground of condemnation. Condemnation rests not solely on Adam's actual sin but also on inborn hereditary corruption and on our further actual and habitual sins; justification rests on Christ's single obedience and never on ours. Hence the justification ground, being unique, is at once first and near; the condemnation ground, sharing the work with many other causes, can be first without having to be near. Sin and condemnation arrive from Adam by natural propagation. The ancient Fathers and the early Reformers met Pelagian imitation with propagation of sin and did not need to mention imputation. Within that propagation Adam is first in the series, yet for each of us he is not the nearest or immediate cause. The sharp contrast: Adam is generation's most remote cause; Christ is regeneration's near cause. We are remote sons of Adam because many generations intervene; believers are near sons of Christ. Faith joins us to Christ directly, and so does his one Spirit shared by Christ and by us, with no intermediate person between Christ and the believer. Given that the learned man knew this, his wording is surprising. He ends by saying meritorious causes always involve proximity because the merit always works near (ἐγγύς) and with effect. Placeus calls that a showy proof: efficacy itself, like causality, admits remote versus near. Force belongs to each cause, and when the effect follows that force is efficacy; else it would not be a cause at all. Adam did propagate nature and corruption into us with real effect, yet remains only a remote cause of both. He is not himself the meritorious cause of our condemnation but the cause of that cause: hereditary corruption streamed from him as the near/immediate ground of condemnation, and Adam's actual sin caused that corruption. We cannot say the same of Christ — that his obedience caused some further virtue which then justifies us. Memorable difference: Christ's obedience is near to justification; Adam's disobedience is remote to condemnation because corruption stands in between. How then could Adam's actual sin be both meritorious and near as our condemnation's cause? If that sin is ours only by imputation, it earns our condemnation only through imputation's intervening act. So it is meritorious not through itself but only accidentally, by that divine, supernatural, voluntary imputing act; Christ's obedience, by contrast, is meritorious through itself, done on purpose by our surety in our stead. It would follow that our sinfulness and condemnation attach through themselves to that divine act and only accidentally to Adam's sin — a conclusion Placeus's conscience will not accept. Further: imputing sin to a man assumes he exists; condemning him to death assumes he lives. Our existing and living naturally precede condemnation, and of those Adam is only remote; so how is he proximate for the condemnation itself?

49: Besides the aberration from the argument there are other vices in the three responses of D. Garissoles, which I will point out in a few words. 1. "We," he says, "contend that there was a certain cause why the Apostle should speak of that imputation. For when he had said that by one man's sin death was brought into the world (Romans 5:12), it could be asked whence that force to that sin, that it brought so great an evil not upon one or another but upon all: Paul answers that it came about thence, that by that one sin all were made liable, or that that one sinning, all are to be understood to have sinned in him and with him." This response, besides that it does not touch the nerve of the argument, makes the Apostle trifling: with only the words changed he answers the very thing that was being asked, and brings forward as the cause of the effect the effect itself whose cause was being sought. For what is it, to the author of this response, that sin entered into the world? nothing, except that actual sin was imputed to all men. That is clearest from this very chapter 8, §. 8, p. 217 of his, and from some other places. What again is it to him that all sinned in Adam? that, he says, can certainly not be better expounded than if we say that Adam's sin is imputed to all — the same chapter, §. 10, p. 222. To one asking, therefore, why Adam's actual sin is imputed to all unto death, the Apostle will have answered: because it is imputed to all. To one asking whence that force to that sin, that it is imputed not to one or another but to all, he answers that it came about thence, that it is imputed to all. What is it to trifle, if this is not?
50: To those two vices a third also is added. For he contradicts himself. For if that was the mind of the Apostle which this response attributes to him, certainly the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (Romans 5:12) ought to be construed after all the antecedents — "sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all" — for they would answer the question that could arise from those immediately preceding words. That overturns the version "in which." For with that version posited, the words "in which all sinned" ought to be construed before all those: for they cohere immediately with the noun ἀνθρώπου, and there is a transposition. So they ought to be construed: "As through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all men" (Romans 5:12).
51: The second response likewise sins by ignorance of the argument, and takes the uncertain cause otherwise than it ought, and besides has some things less rightly said. "Who will have said," he says, "that an uncertain cause is proposed by Paul, when in 1 Corinthians 15:22 he ascends as far as Adam the first-formed, and says that we all die in Adam?" What is the point of this? Does the Apostle there bring forward some cause why all die by the force of the communion they have with Adam? Or are those words, "in Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22), to be understood even imputatively, as they speak? Worse are the things that follow. "Namely," he says, "neither there nor here does the Apostle properly look to particular causes that can reside in each individual of the human race and on account of which it comes about that they die; but he sets out a general cause that looks upon all in the genus equally," and so on. He speaks just as if hereditary corruption were not a general cause looking upon all men equally — when yet that is as common as the death of those who have sinned is common, as human nature is common to them, indeed as imputation is said to be common. So little by little the doctrine of the force and guilt of hereditary corruption, which the first reformers defended with highest zeal, is neglected and nearly blotted out, that it may give place to that imputation which those great men either altogether did not know, or even refuted.
52: "Nor is it fair," he adds, "that we should say that cause is remote and far off, because here one must look not to spaces of years and ages, but to the efficacy of the thing." What? is an injustice that did not stick in me, but in Adam alone, dead some thousands of years before I existed, a cause equally immediate and proximate to me or to my death, as that which inheres in me most inwardly and is by the confession of all the cause of my death? Did not corruption also follow Adam's sin, and death this? corruption is therefore a nearer cause of death than the sin that stuck in Adam alone. "Nor indeed," he subjoins, "do those who say corruption is derived from Adam propose Adam on that account as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — namely, because there is for us with him a most near union by reason of blood, though not by reason of person." On the contrary they propose him as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — that is, the first, from which it flowed out to all others. Therefore that blood is here distinguished from person, and that by reason of the former, not of the latter, a most near union with Adam is said to be ours — that for my part I do not understand. For my blood differs from blood, and my nature from nature, as much as person from Adam's person: the difference of each alike is numerical, not specific. And as I drew my person, so also my nature, through all my intermediate parents from Adam. For Adam is our father not nearest but first; and I have received, or could receive, nothing from him except through my nearest parents.
53: "But," he says, "since a comparison is here instituted between Christ and Adam, the disobedience committed by Adam is no more to be called a remote cause of our condemnation than the obedience performed by Christ is to be called a remote cause of our justification." As if a comparison could not be instituted between two causes of opposite effects, when they are first in their kind, unless each alike is proximate! Who does not know that Christ's obedience is the adequate and only cause of our justification, but Adam's disobedience only an inadequate and partial cause of our condemnation? for we are condemned not on account of Adam's actual sin alone, but also on account of the hereditary corruption inhering in us, and all our other sins whether actual or habitual; whereas yet we are justified on account of Christ's one obedience, and in no way on account of ours. This cause, therefore, since it is the sole and only cause of justification, is the same both first and proximate; but that, since it is not alone, but together with it there are many other causes of condemnation, is first in such a way that there is no necessity that it be proximate. What? do we not draw sin and, through sin, condemnation from Adam by natural propagation? Did not both the Fathers of old and our first Reformers use to oppose the propagation of sin to Pelagian imitation, with no mention made of imputation? And yet of natural propagation, in its own kind indeed, Adam is the first cause, but of each of us the nearest or immediate cause he certainly is not. Here therefore the greatest difference is seen between Adam and Christ. Adam is the most remote cause of our generation, whereas Christ is the proximate cause of our regeneration. We are sons of Adam not nearest but remote: for between us and Adam many others are interposed; but we are nearest sons of Christ, as many as believe in him. For by faith we are united to Christ straight and immediately, and also by his Spirit, who, since he is only one in number both in Christ and in all of us, couples us to Christ so immediately that between Christ and the believer there is no middle person. Since the learned man was not ignorant of these things, how could he speak so? "Finally in meritorious causes," he says, "of the kind we are dealing with, there is always proximity, because that merit always acts near (ἐγγύς) and efficaciously." A fine argument! as if efficacy, like cause, could not equally be distinguished into remote and proximate! for each cause has its own force, and when the effect follows, that is efficacy; otherwise it would not be a cause. Did not Adam efficaciously propagate his nature and corruption into us? And yet he is only a remote cause of our nature and corruption. But he himself is not the meritorious cause of our condemnation, but the cause of this cause; for from him flowed the hereditary corruption that is the proximate or immediate cause of our condemnation, and of this the cause was Adam's actual sin. Can we likewise say that Christ's obedience was the cause of some virtue or obedience that is the cause of our justification? To that extent, therefore, there is a memorable difference between Christ's obedience and Adam's disobedience, and the former is to be called the proximate cause of justification, the latter the remote cause of our condemnation (for corruption is interposed). Otherwise how could Adam's actual sin be a meritorious and proximate cause of our condemnation? First, if it is not ours except by imputation, it does not merit our condemnation except by the intervention of imputation. It is therefore not a meritorious cause of our condemnation through itself, but only through an accident, by reason of that imputation, which is a divine action, and so supernatural and voluntary: whereas yet Christ's obedience is a meritorious cause of our justification through itself; namely, performed to that end and counsel by our surety in our place. That granted, it follows that our being sinners and being condemned is to be ascribed through itself to that divine action, but to Adam's sin only through an accident — which my conscience will in no way let me be led to believe or do. Next, he who imputes sin to some man presupposes that that man exists; he who condemns to death presupposes that he whom he condemns lives. Since therefore of our existing and living, which by nature precedes our condemnation, Adam is only a remote cause, how can he be the proximate cause of our condemnation?
